related_questions.question: Is spinal muscular atrophy a genetic motor neuron disease?
related_questions.snippet: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive disorder that is the leading genetic cause of infantile death. SMA is characterized by loss of motor neurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, leading to weakness and muscle atrophy.

related_questions.question: What is the cause of spinal muscle atrophy?
related_questions.snippet: Spinal muscle atrophy is a genetic disorder. Most forms of SMA are caused by mutations of the survival motor neuron 1 gene (SMN1) on the fifth chromosome, resulting in insufficient expression levels of the SMN protein.

related_questions.question: Can spinal muscular atrophy be cured?
related_questions.snippet: As yet, there is no complete cure for SMA. However, the discovery of the genetic cause of SMA has led to the development of several treatment options that affect the genes involved in SMA — a gene replacement therapy called Zolgensma, and two drugs, called nusinersen (Spinraza) and risdiplam (Evyrsdi).
related_questions.title: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) - Boston Children's Hospital

related_questions.question: How long do people with spinal muscular atrophy live?
related_questions.snippet: The life expectancy of someone with SMA largely depends on the type: SMA type 0 results in death at birth or within one month of life. SMA type 1 often results in death by the age of 2 without breathing support. Life expectancy for SMA type 2 varies but is usually between 20 and 40 years.

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, that's correct. Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder that affects the motor neurons, which are nerve cells responsible for controlling muscle movement. Specifically, SMA impairs the communication between these motor neurons and the muscles, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy (wasting away).
snippet_highlighted_words: SMA impairs the communication between these motor neurons and the muscles, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy (wasting away)

list.title: Genetic Basis:
list.snippet: SMA is caused by a mutation in the SMN1 gene, which is crucial for producing the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein.

list.title: Motor Neuron Impact:
list.snippet: This protein is vital for the health and function of motor neurons, particularly those located in the spinal cord. When there's a deficiency in SMN protein, these motor neurons can shrink and eventually die.

list.title: Communication Breakdown:
list.snippet: As motor neurons die off, the brain's ability to send signals to the muscles is compromised. This leads to muscle weakness and atrophy.

list.title: Muscle Weakness and Atrophy:
list.snippet: The muscles, deprived of nerve signals, weaken and may start to waste away, causing various degrees of physical disability depending on the severity of the SMA.

list.title: Variable Severity:
list.snippet: The severity of SMA symptoms can vary widely, with some individuals experiencing severe muscle weakness from infancy and others developing milder symptoms later in life.
